Content:
If we know the moment-generating function (MGF) for a random variable [MATH: X,] then we can easily find the MGF for any linear transformation of [MATH: X] using the following theorem:

Content:
> If [MATH: Y = aX+b,] where [MATH: X] is a random variable with the MGF [MATH: M_X(t),] then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is
> [MATH: M_Y(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at).]

Content:
For example, consider a binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim B(0.3, 4),] which has the MGF
[MATH: M_X(t) = (0.7 + 0.3e^t)^4.]

Content:
If we have another random variable [MATH: Y = 5X+6,] then we can use the theorem above to conclude that the MGF for [MATH: Y] is
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= e^{6t}M_{X}(5t); = e^{6t}M_{X}(5t); = e^{6t}(0.7 + 0.3e^{5t})^{4}.]

Content:
To see where this theorem comes from, we apply the definition of the MGF:

Content:
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= E[e^{tY}]; = E[e^{t(aX + b)}]; = E[e^{taX} ⋅ e^{tb}]; = e^{tb} ⋅ E[e^{(at)X}]; = e^{tb} ⋅ M_{X}(at).]
Note that for a fixed value of [MATH: t,] we have that [MATH: e^{tb}] is constant (i.e., it does not depend on [MATH: X]), which allows us to take it outside the expectation operator.

You're given that if [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda),] the moment-generating function (MGF) of [MATH: X] is [MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \qquad t < \lambda.]

Let [MATH: Y = 3X+2,] where [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(2).] What is the MGF of [MATH: Y] for [MATH: t < \dfrac23?]

[MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \qquad t < \lambda.]

Let [MATH: Y = 3X+2,] where [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(2).] What is the MGF of [MATH: Y] for [MATH: t < \dfrac23?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: Y = aX+b,] where [MATH: X] is a random variable with the MGF [MATH: M_X(t),] then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is [MATH: M_Y(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at).]

For an exponential random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda),] we have [MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \qquad t < \lambda.]

In our case, since [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(2),] we have [MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{2}{2 - t}, \qquad t < 2.]

Therefore, since [MATH: Y = 3X+2,] we have

[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= e^{2t}M_{X}(3t); = e^{2t} ⋅ (2)/(2 − 3t); = (2e^{2t})/(2 − 3t),] where we assume that [MATH: 3t < 2.] Finally, we get

[MATH: M_{Y}(t) = (2e^{2t})/(2 − 3t), t < (2)/(3).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
If we know the moment-generating functions (MGFs) for independent random variables [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2,] then we can easily find the MGF for their sum using the following theorem:

Content:
> If [MATH: Y = X_1 + X_2,] where [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent random variables with MGF's [MATH: M_{X_1}(t)] and [MATH: M_{X_2}(t),] respectively, then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is
> [MATH: M_Y(t) = M_{X_1}(t) M_{X_2}(t).]

Content:
Let's prove this when [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are continuous (the proof is similar for discrete random variables). We start with the definition of the MGF:

Content:
[MATH: M_Y(t) = \textrm E \left[ e^{tY} \right] = \textrm E \left[ e^{t(X_1 + X_2)} \right]]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: X_1] defined on [MATH: [a,b]] and [MATH: X_2] is defined on [MATH: [c,d],] then by the definition of the expected value, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E \left[ e^{t(X_1 + X_2)} \right] = \int_c^d \int_a^b f_{X_1,X_2} (x_1, x_2) e^{t(x_1 + x_2)} \, \textrm dx_1 \textrm dx_2,]

Content:
where [MATH: f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)] is the joint probability density function of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2.]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, we have

Content:
[MATH: f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2) = f_{X_1}(x_1) f_{X_2}(x_2),]

Content:
and therefore

Content:
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}, X_{2}}(x_{1}, x_{2})e^{t(x_{1} + x_{2})}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{t(x_{1} + x_{2})}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{tx_{1}}e^{tx_{2}}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})e^{tx_{1}}dx_{1} ⋅ ∫_{c}^{d}f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{tx_{2}}dx_{2}; = E[e^{tX_{1}}] ⋅ E[e^{tX_{2}}]; = M_{X_{1}}(t)M_{X_{2}}(t).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
If we know the moment-generating function (MGF) for a random variable [MATH: X,] then we can easily find the MGF for any linear transformation of [MATH: X] using the following theorem:

Content:
> If [MATH: Y = aX+b,] where [MATH: X] is a random variable with the MGF [MATH: M_X(t),] then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is
> [MATH: M_Y(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at).]

Content:
For example, consider a binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim B(0.3, 4),] which has the MGF
[MATH: M_X(t) = (0.7 + 0.3e^t)^4.]

Content:
If we have another random variable [MATH: Y = 5X+6,] then we can use the theorem above to conclude that the MGF for [MATH: Y] is
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= e^{6t}M_{X}(5t); = e^{6t}M_{X}(5t); = e^{6t}(0.7 + 0.3e^{5t})^{4}.]

Content:
To see where this theorem comes from, we apply the definition of the MGF:

Content:
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= E[e^{tY}]; = E[e^{t(aX + b)}]; = E[e^{taX} ⋅ e^{tb}]; = e^{tb} ⋅ E[e^{(at)X}]; = e^{tb} ⋅ M_{X}(at).]
Note that for a fixed value of [MATH: t,] we have that [MATH: e^{tb}] is constant (i.e., it does not depend on [MATH: X]), which allows us to take it outside the expectation operator.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the MGF of a Linearly Transformed Random Variable

Example Prompt:
You're given that if [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda),] the moment-generating function (MGF) of [MATH: X] is
[MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \qquad t < \lambda.]

Let [MATH: Y = 3X+2,] where [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(2).] What is the MGF of [MATH: Y] for [MATH: t < \dfrac23?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: Y = aX+b,] where [MATH: X] is a random variable with the MGF [MATH: M_X(t),] then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is
[MATH: M_Y(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at).]

For an exponential random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(\lambda),] we have
[MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \qquad t < \lambda.]

In our case, since [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Exp}(2),] we have
[MATH: M_X(t) = \dfrac{2}{2 - t}, \qquad t < 2.]

Therefore, since [MATH: Y = 3X+2,] we have

[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= e^{2t}M_{X}(3t); = e^{2t} ⋅ (2)/(2 − 3t); = (2e^{2t})/(2 − 3t),]
where we assume that [MATH: 3t < 2.] Finally, we get

[MATH: M_{Y}(t) = (2e^{2t})/(2 − 3t), t < (2)/(3).]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Sums of Independent Random Variables

Content:
If we know the moment-generating functions (MGFs) for independent random variables [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2,] then we can easily find the MGF for their sum using the following theorem:

Content:
> If [MATH: Y = X_1 + X_2,] where [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent random variables with MGF's [MATH: M_{X_1}(t)] and [MATH: M_{X_2}(t),] respectively, then the MGF of [MATH: Y] is
> [MATH: M_Y(t) = M_{X_1}(t) M_{X_2}(t).]

Content:
Let's prove this when [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are continuous (the proof is similar for discrete random variables). We start with the definition of the MGF:

Content:
[MATH: M_Y(t) = \textrm E \left[ e^{tY} \right] = \textrm E \left[ e^{t(X_1 + X_2)} \right]]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: X_1] defined on [MATH: [a,b]] and [MATH: X_2] is defined on [MATH: [c,d],] then by the definition of the expected value, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E \left[ e^{t(X_1 + X_2)} \right] = \int_c^d \int_a^b f_{X_1,X_2} (x_1, x_2) e^{t(x_1 + x_2)} \, \textrm dx_1 \textrm dx_2,]

Content:
where [MATH: f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)] is the joint probability density function of [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2.]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are independent, we have

Content:
[MATH: f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2) = f_{X_1}(x_1) f_{X_2}(x_2),]

Content:
and therefore

Content:
[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}, X_{2}}(x_{1}, x_{2})e^{t(x_{1} + x_{2})}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{t(x_{1} + x_{2})}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{tx_{1}}e^{tx_{2}}dx_{1}dx_{2}; = ∫_{a}^{b}f_{X_{1}}(x_{1})e^{tx_{1}}dx_{1} ⋅ ∫_{c}^{d}f_{X_{2}}(x_{2})e^{tx_{2}}dx_{2}; = E[e^{tX_{1}}] ⋅ E[e^{tX_{2}}]; = M_{X_{1}}(t)M_{X_{2}}(t).]

---

For a Poisson random variable [MATH: X_1 \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda),] we have

In our case, since [MATH: X_1 \sim \textrm{Po}(4),] we have

Then, since [MATH: X_2 \sim \textrm{Po}(7),] we have

Therefore, we have

EXPLANATION

Explanation:

[MATH: M_Y(t) = M_{X_1}(a_1t) M_{X_2}(a_2t).]

Here, we're given [MATH: Y = 8X_1 - 2X_2,] so we have

[MATH: M_X(t) = (1-2t)^{-k/2}, \qquad t < \dfrac12.]

[MATH: M_{X_{1}}(t)|= (1 − 2t)^{− 2}, t < (1)/(2); M_{X_{1}}(8t)|= (1)/((1 − 16t)^{2}), t < (1)/(16).]

[MATH: M_{X_{2}}(t)|= (1 − 2t)^{− 1}, t < (1)/(2); M_{X_{2}}(− 2t)|= (1)/((1 + 4t)), t > − (1)/(4).]

Therefore, for [MATH: -\dfrac14 < t < \dfrac1{16} ,] we have

[MATH: M_{Y}(t)|= (1)/((1 − 16t)^{2}(1 + 4t)).]
